title: Foundations of Human Nutrition

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of your body like a car. Macronutrients are the big tank of gasoline you pour in by the gallon to make the engine go, while micronutrients are the tiny drops of oil that keep the parts working. 'Macro' means big, so macronutrients are the big, energy-giving foods: carbs, proteins, and fats.

### Question 2

Some things your body is like a little factory for and can build on its own. But a few important parts it just cannot manufacture, so you HAVE to eat them, kind of like a recipe that calls for an ingredient you can only get from the store. Those must-eat ingredients are the 'essential' nutrients.

### Question 3

Imagine packing a suitcase. Fat is like a super-compressed bag that stuffs the most energy into the smallest space, giving 9 calories in each gram, while carbs and protein only pack about 4. That is why your body loves to store extra energy as fat: it fits a lot into a little.

### Question 4

Protein is like a box of LEGO bricks. Your body pulls the bricks (amino acids) out of the box and snaps them together to build muscles and fix parts that get worn out. You can burn the bricks for heat in an emergency, but that would be a waste; their real job is building.

### Question 5

Fat-soluble vitamins are like guests who move into your house and stay, so if too many show up it gets crowded and causes trouble (toxicity). Water-soluble vitamins are like guests who leave the same day, washing out in your pee, so you need to keep inviting new ones but they rarely overcrowd.

### Question 6

Picture a bank account for energy. If you put in more money (calories eaten) than you spend (calories burned), the balance grows and gets stored as fat. 'Positive' just means the account is filling up because more is coming in than going out.

### Question 7

Water does not give you energy like food, but it is the river everything floats on inside your body: it carries stuff around, helps chemical reactions happen, and cools you down when you sweat. Your body makes only a tiny bit of its own water and you lose it all day, so you must keep refilling, which is why it is 'essential.'

### Question 8

Each food on the plate has a main job. Oil is basically liquid fat, so its job is fat. Rice brings the carbs, chicken brings the protein, and veggies bring the fiber and vitamins. The trick is spotting which food is the 'star player' for each nutrient.

### Question 9

Vitamins are like batteries your body keeps in a drawer. If you stop restocking, the drawer slowly empties until the gadgets that need those batteries stop working, and that breakdown is a deficiency disease. A different vitamin cannot fill in, because each one runs its own specific gadgets.

### Question 10

Each gram of fat carries 9 calories, but each gram of carb or protein carries only 4. So even though there are more grams of carbs here, the fat still packs a bigger punch, and 10 grams of fat easily beats 5 grams of protein. It is like comparing heavy coins to light ones: fewer heavy coins can add up to more.

### Question 11

Protein is your building crew, but if the furnace runs out of firewood (carbs and fat), the body starts burning the crew's LEGO bricks just to stay warm. When you eat enough carbs and fat, the crew gets to keep building instead of being thrown in the fire. That rescue is called 'protein sparing.'

### Question 12

Imagine two backpacks that weigh exactly the same. The yogurt-and-fruit backpack is packed with useful gear (vitamins and minerals), while the sugary snack bar is stuffed mostly with foam that adds weight (calories) but does nothing helpful. Getting more useful gear for the same weight is what 'nutrient-dense' means.
